gancho: Para medir a idade da Terra, 4,55 bilhões de anos, Clair Patterson teve de caçar chumbo que contaminava tudo, até o próprio cabelo. A caçada virou uma luta contra a gasolina com chumbo.
explicacao: A partir de 1948, em Chicago, o geoquímico americano Clair Patterson (1922–1995) tentava medir o chumbo de cristais de zircão, enquanto o colega George Tilton media o urânio. Os resultados dele vinham sempre com chumbo "demais": o laboratório inteiro estava contaminado, inclusive o cabelo do pesquisador. Ao se mudar para o Caltech, em 1953, ele montou um laboratório do zero, vedou as entradas de ar, lavou os aparelhos com ácido e destilou os reagentes que recebia. Criou assim uma das primeiras salas limpas. Com o chumbo do meteorito Canyon Diablo, publicou em 1956 a idade de 4,55 bilhões de anos, que segue praticamente sem contestação; até então, a estimativa corrente era de uns 3,3 bilhões. A obsessão pela contaminação tomou o resto da vida dele. Em amostras de gelo da Groenlândia e da Antártida, viu que o chumbo na atmosfera começou a subir depois da adoção do chumbo tetraetila nos combustíveis. Mostrou ainda que ossos modernos tinham de 700 a 1.200 vezes mais chumbo que esqueletos peruanos de 1.600 anos. Ao bater de frente com a indústria, perdeu contratos de pesquisa e, em 1971, ficou fora de um painel oficial sobre o tema. A gasolina com chumbo para carros foi proibida nos EUA em 1996, e no fim dos anos 1990 o chumbo no sangue dos americanos tinha caído até 80%.

fontes.trecho: (born Claire Cameron Patterson Jr.; June 2, 1922 – December 5, 1995) was an American geochemist. [...] By using lead isotopic data from the Canyon Diablo meteorite, he calculated an age for the Earth of 4.55 billion years, a figure far more accurate than estimates existing at the time and one that has remained largely unchallenged since 1956. [...] Patterson discovered that lead contamination was pervasive throughout his laboratory, even in his own hair. [...] Tilton measured the uranium and Patterson the types and amounts of lead. [...] After beginning their work in 1948, Patterson soon noted that his lead samples were being contaminated. [...] but Patterson's data typically was skewed with "too much" lead. [...] In 1953, Brown and Patterson arrived at Caltech, where Patterson was authorized to build his own lab from scratch. He proceeded to secure all points of entry from air and other contaminants. He acid-cleaned all apparatuses and even distilled all chemicals shipped to him. In essence, Patterson created one of the first laboratory clean rooms [...] Before his paper, it was largely believed the Earth was around 3.3 billion years old. [...] He determined—by analysing ice-core samples from Camp Century in Greenland taken in 1964 and from Antarctica in 1965—that atmospheric lead levels had begun to increase steadily and dangerously soon after tetraethyl lead (TEL) was introduced [...] he devoted the rest of his life to eliminating lead from being introduced into the environment. [...] Following his criticism of the lead industry, he was refused contracts by several supposedly-neutral research organizations, including the United States Public Health Service. In 1971 he was excluded from a National Research Council (NRC) panel on atmospheric lead contamination [...] He compared levels of lead, barium, and calcium in 1600-year-old Peruvian skeletons and showed a 700- to 1200-fold increase in lead levels of modern human bones [...] Leaded automotive gasoline was finally completely banned in the USA on January 1, 1996 [...] By the late 1990s, lead levels in the blood of Americans were reported to have dropped by up to 80%.

gancho: Das 14 vacinas de rotina recomendadas nos EUA quando Maurice Hilleman morreu, em 2005, oito saíram da equipe dele, um nome que quase ninguém conhece. A da caxumba nasceu do vírus que ele colheu da filha doente, em 1963.
explicacao: O microbiologista americano Maurice Hilleman (1919–2005) desenvolveu mais de 40 vacinas, a maior parte na farmacêutica Merck. Das 14 vacinas recomendadas de rotina no calendário americano na época da morte dele, a equipe dele criou oito: sarampo, caxumba, hepatites A e B, catapora e três bactérias, o meningococo, o pneumococo e o Haemophilus influenzae. Mesmo assim, nenhuma vacina ou descoberta leva o nome dele. A da caxumba tem uma origem doméstica: em 1963, a filha Jeryl Lynn ficou doente, e Hilleman cultivou o vírus a partir de material colhido dela. A cepa Jeryl Lynn ainda é usada, inclusive na vacina tríplice contra sarampo, caxumba e rubéola, que ele também desenvolveu e que foi a primeira aprovada com vários vírus vivos. Em 1957, ele estava entre os primeiros a perceber que um surto de gripe em Hong Kong podia virar pandemia; 40 milhões de doses de vacina foram preparadas. Segundo uma estimativa, as vacinas dele salvam quase oito milhões de vidas por ano. Robert Gallo, um dos descobridores do HIV, disse que não conhecia ninguém que tivesse feito mais pela saúde humana com menos reconhecimento.

fontes.trecho: Maurice Ralph Hilleman (August 30, 1919 – April 11, 2005) was a leading American microbiologist who specialized in vaccinology and developed over 40 vaccines, an unparalleled record of productivity. According to one estimate, his vaccines save nearly eight million lives each year. [...] Of the 14 vaccines routinely recommended in American vaccine schedules, Hilleman and his team developed eight: those for measles, mumps, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, chickenpox, Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae bacteria. [...] It was at Merck that Hilleman developed most of the forty experimental and licensed animal and human vaccines for which he is credited [...] Hilleman was among the first to recognize that a 1957 outbreak of influenza in Hong Kong could become a huge pandemic. [...] Forty million doses of vaccines were prepared and distributed. [...] In 1963, his daughter Jeryl Lynn came down with the mumps. He cultivated material from her, and used it as the basis of a mumps vaccine. The Jeryl Lynn strain of the mumps vaccine is still used. The strain is used in the trivalent (measles, mumps and rubella) MMR vaccine that he also developed, the first approved vaccine to incorporate multiple live virus strains. [...] None of his vaccines or discoveries are named after him. [...] Robert Gallo, co-discoverer of HIV (the virus that causes AIDS), said in 2005: "If I had to name a person who has done more for the benefit of human health, with less recognition than anyone else, it would be Maurice Hilleman. [...] In 2007, Anthony S. Fauci wrote in a biographical memoir of Hilleman: [...] Of the fourteen vaccines currently recommended in the United States, Maurice developed eight.

gancho: Em 1774, 22 anos antes de Edward Jenner, um fazendeiro inglês arranhou os braços da mulher e dos filhos com material de uma vaca doente para protegê-los da varíola. Os vizinhos o vaiavam nas feiras.
explicacao: No interior leiteiro da Inglaterra, era saber popular que quem pegava a varíola bovina, uma doença branda passada pelas tetas das vacas, ficava imune à varíola humana. Benjamin Jesty, fazendeiro em Yetminster, no condado de Dorset, já tinha tido a doença das vacas, assim como duas empregadas. Quando uma epidemia de varíola chegou à vila, em 1774, ele levou a mulher, Elizabeth, e os dois filhos mais velhos até uma vaca doente numa fazenda vizinha e, com uma agulha de cerzir, passou o material das feridas do animal arranhando o braço deles. Os meninos tiveram reações leves; o braço da mulher inflamou muito, mas ela também se recuperou. A vizinhança o chamou de desumano, e alguns temiam virar bichos com chifres. Nos anos seguintes, os filhos foram expostos à varíola e não adoeceram. Jesty não divulgou o que fez, e o crédito ficou com o médico Edward Jenner, que começou seus experimentos em 1796 e recebeu do Parlamento 10 mil libras em 1802 e mais 20 mil em 1807. Jesty não foi o único nem o primeiro: há registros de outras pessoas que fizeram o mesmo naquelas décadas. Em 1805, chamado a Londres, o filho mais velho aceitou ser inoculado de novo com varíola para provar que continuava imune.

fontes.trecho: Unlike Edward Jenner, a medical doctor who is given broad credit for developing the smallpox vaccine in 1796, Jesty did not publicise his findings made some twenty years earlier in 1774. [...] It was known in the dairy-farming areas in the south-west of the country that the milkmaids and other workers who contracted cowpox from handling cows' udders, were afterwards immune to smallpox. [...] Jesty and two of his female servants, Ann Notley and Mary Reade, had been infected with cowpox. When an epidemic of smallpox came to Yetminster in 1774, Jesty decided to try to give his wife Elizabeth and two eldest sons immunity by infecting them with cowpox. He took his family to a cow at a farm in nearby Chetnole that had the disease, and using a darning needle, transferred pustular material from the cow by scratching their arms. The boys had mild local reactions and quickly recovered but his wife's arm became very inflamed and for a time her condition gave cause for concern, although she too recovered fully in time. [...] He was labelled inhuman, and was "hooted at, reviled and pelted whenever he attended markets in the neighbourhood'". The introduction of an animal disease into a human body was thought disgusting and some even "feared their metamorphosis into horned beasts". But the treatment's efficacy was several times demonstrated in the years which followed, when Jesty's two elder sons, exposed to smallpox, failed to catch the disease. [...] Jesty was one of six English, Danish and German people (Sevel, Jensen and Jesty in 1774, Rendall and Plett in 1791) who reportedly administered cowpox to artificially induce immunity against smallpox from 1770 to 1791; only Jobst Bose of Göttingen, Germany, with his 1769 inoculations pre-dated Jesty's work. [...] In June 1802 Jenner was given a reward of £10,000 from the House of Commons for discovering and promoting vaccination, and another award of £20,000 followed in 1807. [...] work which pre-dated Jenner's by 22 years. [...] In 1805, at Pearson's instigation and the institution's invitation, Jesty gave his evidence [...] Robert, Jesty's oldest son (by then 28 years old) also made the trip to London and agreed to be inoculated with smallpox again to prove that he still had immunity.

gancho: Às vésperas da Segunda Guerra, um corretor da bolsa londrino ajudou a tirar 669 crianças, quase todas judias, da Tchecoslováquia. O feito ficou quase 50 anos esquecido, até a mulher dele achar um álbum no sótão.
explicacao: No fim de 1938, Nicholas Winton trocou uma viagem de esqui na Suíça por uma visita a Praga, a pedido de um amigo que ajudava refugiados. Ficou só umas três semanas. De volta a Londres, cuidou das exigências britânicas: cada criança com menos de 17 anos precisava de um lugar para ficar e de uma garantia de 50 libras. Para achar famílias dispostas a recebê-las, publicava fotos delas na revista Picture Post. No total, encontrou lares para 669 crianças; muitos dos pais morreram em Auschwitz. O último grupo, de 250 crianças, deveria sair de Praga em 1º de setembro de 1939, o dia em que a Alemanha invadiu a Polônia, e não partiu; só duas delas sobreviveram à guerra. Winton fazia questão de citar os voluntários que ficaram em Praga, como Trevor Chadwick e Doreen Warriner. Depois, a história quase sumiu. Em 1988, a mulher dele achou no sótão um álbum com as listas das crianças e das famílias que as acolheram. Naquele ano, no programa That's Life!, da BBC, Winton foi apresentado a pessoas que tinha salvado. Num programa seguinte, mais de vinte pessoas sentadas ao redor dele se levantaram: eram crianças que ele ajudara a resgatar. Ele morreu em 2015, aos 106 anos.

fontes.trecho: Sir Nicholas George Winton (né Wertheim; 19 May 1909 – 1 July 2015) was a British stockbroker and humanitarian [...] Winton assisted in the rescue of 669 children from Czechoslovakia on the eve of the Second World War. [...] His humanitarian accomplishments remained unknown and unnoticed by the world for nearly 50 years until 1988 when he was invited to the BBC television programme That's Life!, where he was reunited with dozens of the children he had helped come to Britain [...] Winton died in 2015, aged 106. [...] Shortly before Christmas 1938, Winton was planning to travel to Switzerland for a skiing holiday. [...] he decided instead to visit Prague and help Martin Blake [...] Altogether, Winton spent three weeks  in Prague and left in January 1939 [...] the House of Commons approved a measure to allow the entry into Britain of refugees younger than 17, provided they had a place to stay and a warranty of £50 [...] Winton ultimately found homes in Britain for 669 children, many of whose parents perished in the Auschwitz concentration camp. [...] Throughout the summer of 1939, he placed photographs of the children in Picture Post seeking families to accept them. [...] The last group of children, scheduled to leave Prague on 1 September 1939, was unable to depart. With Hitler's invasion of Poland on the same day, the Second World War had begun. Of the 250 children due to leave on that train, only two survived the war. Winton acknowledged the vital roles in Prague of Doreen Warriner, Trevor Chadwick, [...] until in 1988 his wife found a detailed scrapbook in their attic, containing lists of the children, including their parents' names and the names and addresses of the families that took them in. [...] In a later, follow-up That's Life! programme at which Winton was also in the audience, Rantzen asked whether anybody in the audience was among the children who owed their lives to Winton, and if so, to stand: more than two dozen people surrounding Winton rose and applauded.

gancho: Em 1940, o cônsul português em Bordeaux desobedeceu à ditadura de Salazar e deu vistos a milhares de refugiados do nazismo. Foi punido, morreu pobre, e o regime depois posou de porto seguro.
explicacao: Aristides de Sousa Mendes (1885–1954) tinha sido cônsul em vários países, inclusive no Brasil, em Curitiba, São Luís e Porto Alegre. Em 1938 assumiu o consulado-geral em Bordeaux, na França. Em novembro de 1939, uma circular de Lisboa mandou os cônsules barrarem refugiados considerados "inconvenientes", entre eles judeus expulsos de seus países e apátridas. Sousa Mendes começou a desobedecer quase de imediato. Em junho de 1940, com os alemães avançando e Bordeaux lotada de refugiados, ele anunciou, segundo o filho, que daria vistos a todos, sem distinção de nacionalidade, raça ou religião, e montou uma linha de produção com a mulher, os filhos e alguns refugiados. O embaixador português na Espanha o declarou mentalmente incapaz e anulou os vistos. Chamado de volta a Lisboa, ele ainda guiou com o carro oficial um grupo de refugiados até um posto de fronteira que não tinha telefone. Salazar o condenou a um ano de inatividade com meio salário e à aposentadoria forçada. Sem conseguir emprego, Sousa Mendes morreu na pobreza em 1954. Depois da guerra, Salazar assumiu o mérito por Portugal ter acolhido os refugiados. O historiador Yehuda Bauer chamou o feito do cônsul de talvez a maior ação de resgate de um único indivíduo no Holocausto. Portugal só o reabilitou em 1988.

fontes.trecho: July 19, 1885 – April 3, 1954) was a Portuguese diplomat [...] As the Portuguese consul-general in the French city of Bordeaux, he defied the orders of António de Oliveira Salazar's Estado Novo regime, issuing visas to thousands of refugees fleeing Nazi-occupied France, including Jews. [...] He was unable to find other employment and died in poverty in 1954. [...] Holocaust scholar Yehuda Bauer characterized Sousa Mendes' deeds as "perhaps the largest rescue action by a single individual during the Holocaust." [...] In 1988, the Portuguese national assembly voted unanimously for his rehabilitation and his charges were dismissed. [...] Curitiba (1918–1919), San Francisco (1921-1924), S. Luís do Maranhão (April 1924), Porto Alegre (1924-1926) [...] In 1938, he was assigned to the post of Consul-General of Bordeaux, France [...] On 11 November 1939, the Portuguese government sent Circular 14 to all Portuguese consuls throughout Europe, stating the categories of war refugees whom the PVDE considered to be "inconvenient or dangerous." The categories included “Jews expelled from their countries or those from whence they issue, stateless persons, [...] Sousa Mendes began disobeying Circular 14 almost immediately [...] According to his son Pedro Nuno, "My father got up, and announced in a loud voice: 'From now on I'm giving everyone visas. There will be no more nationalities, races or religions.' [...] After Bordeaux was bombed by the Wehrmacht on the night of 19–20 June 1940, the demand for Portuguese visas intensified [...] He set up an assembly line process, aided by his wife, sons Pedro Nuno and José Antonio, his secretary José Seabra, Rabbi Kruger, and a few other refugees. [...] He declared Sousa Mendes to be mentally incompetent and, acting on Salazar's authority, he invalidated all further visas. [...] Ordering his driver to slow down, Father waved the group to follow him to a border checkpoint that had no telephones. [...] "I sentence Consul First Class, Aristides de Sousa Mendes, to a penalty of one year of inactivity with the right to one half of his rank's pay, being obliged subsequently to be retired." [...] After the war, with the victory of the Allied forces over the Axis, Salazar took credit for Portugal having received the refugees [...] the image of 'Portugal, a safe haven' was born then in Bordeaux

gancho: A droga contra a malária que deu o Nobel de 2015 a Tu Youyou saiu de um projeto secreto da China. A pista estava num livro de 340 d.C., e ela se ofereceu como cobaia antes dos testes em pacientes.
explicacao: Em 1967, o Vietnã do Norte pediu ajuda à China contra uma malária resistente à cloroquina que atingia seus soldados. O premiê Zhou Enlai convenceu Mao a criar um projeto secreto, batizado de Projeto 523 pela data de início, 23 de maio. Em 1969, a farmacêutica Tu Youyou passou a chefiar o grupo do seu instituto. No mundo, mais de 240 mil compostos já tinham sido testados sem sucesso, e ela foi buscar pistas nos clássicos da medicina chinesa: reuniu 640 receitas num caderno, e até 1971 a equipe tinha avaliado mais de 2 mil receitas tradicionais e preparado 380 extratos de ervas. A artemísia-doce (qinghao) prometia, mas falhava quando extraída do jeito tradicional, com água quente. Segundo Tu, a virada veio de um texto escrito em 340 por Ge Hong, que mandava mergulhar um punhado da erva em água, torcer e beber o suco, sem aquecer. Como o calor estraga o princípio ativo, ela propôs extrair com éter a baixa temperatura. Em 1972, a equipe isolou a substância pura, a artemisinina. Como chefe do grupo, Tu se ofereceu como cobaia humana antes dos testes com pacientes, e o trabalho saiu sem nome de autor em 1977. Ela é chamada de "cientista dos três nãos": sem pós-graduação, sem experiência no exterior e fora das academias nacionais de ciências.

fontes.trecho: For her work, Tu received the 2011 Lasker Award in clinical medicine and the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine [...] In 1967, during the Vietnam War, President Ho Chi Minh of North Vietnam asked Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai for help in developing a malaria treatment for his soldiers [...] where a majority came down with a form of malaria which is resistant to chloroquine. [...] Zhou Enlai convinced Mao Zedong to set up a secret drug discovery project named Project 523 after its starting date, 23 May 1967. In early 1969, Tu was appointed head of the Project 523 research group at her institute. [...] Scientists worldwide had screened over 240,000 compounds without success. [...] She first investigated the Chinese medical classics in history [...] Her notebook summarized 640 prescriptions. By 1971, her team had screened over 2,000 traditional Chinese recipes and made 380 herbal extracts, from some 200 herbs, which were tested on mice. [...] At first, it was ineffective because they extracted it with the traditional technique using hot water. [...] Tu says she was influenced by the source, written in 340 by Ge Hong, a scholar from the Jin dynasty, which states that this herb should be steeped in cold water. This book instructed the reader to immerse a handful of qinghao in water, wring out the juice, and drink it all. Since hot water damages the active ingredient in the plant, she proposed a method using low temperature ether to extract the effective compound instead. [...] In 1972, she and her colleagues obtained the pure substance and named it qinghaosu (青蒿素), or artemisinin in English. [...] Tu volunteered to be the first human test subject. "As head of this research group, I had the responsibility," she said. [...] Her work was published anonymously in 1977. [...] Tu is regarded as the "Three-Without Scientist" – no postgraduate degree (there was no postgraduate education then in China), no study or research experience abroad, and not a member of either of the Chinese national academies [...] She had no bad reactions, so she conducted successful clinical trials with human patients.

gancho: Em 1895, em Calcutá, Jagadish Chandra Bose fez micro-ondas atravessarem duas paredes e o corpo do governador de Bengala para tocar uma campainha. Avesso a patentes, ele mostrava a todos como seus detectores funcionavam.
explicacao: Bose (1858–1937) era professor de física em Calcutá e enfrentava discriminação racial e falta de verba e de equipamento. Em 1894, inspirado nas demonstrações do britânico Oliver Lodge, montou um laboratório numa salinha e conseguiu encurtar as ondas de rádio até a escala dos milímetros, para estudar como elas se comportam feito luz. Numa demonstração pública em novembro de 1895, as ondas passaram pelo corpo do governador da província de Bengala e percorreram 23 metros, atravessando duas paredes, até um aparelho que tocou uma campainha. Ele foi o primeiro a usar uma junção de semicondutor, um cristal de galena, para detectar ondas de rádio. Enquanto Marconi corria para transformar o rádio em telégrafo comercial, Bose queria entender o fenômeno. Explicava o detector abertamente nas palestras, e uma patente americana que um amigo o convenceu a tirar acabou caducando por desinteresse. Depois dele, quase ninguém trabalhou com ondas milimétricas por 50 anos. O físico Nevill Mott, Nobel de 1977, disse que Bose estava pelo menos 60 anos à frente do seu tempo. Em 2012, o trabalho dele foi reconhecido como marco histórico pelo IEEE, a associação internacional de engenheiros eletricistas e eletrônicos, o primeiro reconhecimento desse tipo a uma descoberta feita na Índia.

fontes.trecho: 30 November 1858 – 23 November 1937) [...] There, despite racial discrimination and a lack of funding and equipment, Bose carried on his scientific research. [...] Bose became interested in radio following the 1894 publication of British physicist Oliver Lodge's demonstrations on how to transmit and detect radio waves. He began his own research in the new field in November 1894, setting up his equipment in small 20 ft sq room at Presidency College. Wanting to study the light-like properties of radio waves which were hard to study using long radio waves, he managed to reduce the waves to the millimetre level [...] In November 1895 at a public demonstration at the Town Hall of Kolkata, Bose showed how the millimetre range wavelength microwaves could travel through the human body (of Lieutenant Governor Sir William Mackenzie), and over a distance of 23 metres through two intervening walls to a trigger apparatus he had set up to ring a bell [...] Bose's work in radio microwave optics was specifically directed towards studying the nature of the phenomenon and was not an attempt to develop radio into a communication medium. [...] Bose was not interested in patenting his work, and openly revealed the operation of his galena crystal detector in his lectures. A friend in the US persuaded him to take out a US patent on his detector, but he did not actively pursue it and allowed it to lapse. Bose was the first to use a semiconductor junction to detect radio waves [...] In fact, further work at millimetre wavelengths was almost non-existent for the following 50 years. [...] Sir Nevill Mott, Nobel Laureate in 1977 for his own contributions to solid-state electronics, remarked that "J.C. Bose was at least 60 years ahead of his time. [...] On 14 September 2012, Bose's experimental work in millimetre-band radio was recognised as an IEEE Milestone in Electrical and Computer Engineering, the first such recognition of a discovery in India.

gancho: Garrett Morgan, inventor negro, demonstrava seu capuz antifumaça disfarçado de "Big Chief Mason", um falso chefe indígena. Em 1916, usou o capuz para tirar homens de um túnel cheio de gás sob o lago Erie.
explicacao: Filho de ex-escravizados, Garrett Morgan (1877–1963) estudou até a sexta série e virou inventor em Cleveland, nos EUA. O capuz que patenteou usava uma esponja úmida para filtrar a fumaça e um tubo que pendia até perto do chão: como a fumaça quente sobe, o ar de baixo fica mais respirável. Para vender o aparelho, às vezes contratava um ator branco que se passava pelo inventor; em outras, ele mesmo se disfarçava de "Big Chief Mason", um suposto indígena do Canadá, e ficava 20 minutos numa tenda cheia de fumaça preta. Em julho de 1916, uma explosão num túnel de captação de água a 15 metros sob o lago Erie prendeu operários, e duas tentativas de resgate falharam, com os socorristas virando vítimas. Chamado no meio da noite, Morgan chegou às pressas com o irmão Frank, trazendo quatro capuzes. Diante da desconfiança geral, os dois entraram com outros dois voluntários e ajudaram a tirar sobreviventes; depois outros os seguiram. Morgan fez quatro viagens ao túnel, e a saúde dele sofreu por anos. Morgan não recebeu a medalha de heroísmo do Carnegie Hero Fund e atribuiu isso ao racismo. Revendo seus arquivos, o fundo diz que ele foi indicado e recusado porque o capuz reduzia o risco que corria, e que não há prova de motivo racial. Quando a foto dele saiu nos jornais, cidades do sul cancelaram encomendas ao descobrir que o inventor era negro.

fontes.trecho: Garrett Augustus Morgan Sr. (March 4, 1877 – July 27, 1963) was an American inventor [...] His father was Sydney Morgan, a freed slave [...] His mother, also a freed slave, was Elizabeth Reed [...] Morgan received a sixth grade education [...] In 1916, Morgan rescued workers trapped in a water intake tunnel 50 ft (15 m) beneath Lake Erie [...] His device used a moist sponge to filter out smoke and cool the air. It took advantage of the way smoke and fumes tend to rise to higher positions while leaving a layer of more breathable air below, by using an air intake tube that dangled near the floor. [...] He was able to sell his invention around the country, sometimes using the tactic of hiring a white actor, who would take credit rather than revealing himself as its inventor. For demonstrations of the device, he sometimes adopted the disguise of "Big Chief Mason", a purported full-blooded Indian from the Walpole Island Indian Reserve in Canada. [...] Disguised as "Big Chief Mason", he would enter the tent full of black smoke, and would remain there for 20 minutes before emerging unharmed. [...] after the July 24, Waterworks Tunnel explosion in Cleveland, Ohio. Before Morgan arrived, two previous rescue attempts had failed. The attempted rescuers had become victims themselves by entering the tunnel and not returning. Morgan was roused in the middle of the night [...] He and his brother Frank, arrived on the scene [...] bringing four Smoke Hoods with them. Most of the rescuers on the scene were initially skeptical of his device, so he and his brother went into the tunnel along with two other volunteers, and pulled out two men from the previous rescue attempts. He emerged carrying a victim on his back, and his brother followed just behind with another. Others joined in after his team succeeded, and rescued several more. [...] Morgan personally made four trips into the tunnel during the rescue, and his health was affected for years afterward from the fumes he encountered there. [...] Morgan believed that the omission was racially motivated. [...] However, the national news contained photographs of him, and officials a number of southern cities canceled their existing orders when they discovered he was black.

fontes.titulo: Behind the Scenes: Shedding Light on the complicated case of Black Inventor Garrett Morgan
fontes.trecho: The safety of Morgan’s gas hood invention enabled him to go into the gas-filled tunnel multiple times to save men who had collapsed from lack of oxygen. [...] With several of his smoke hoods in tow, Morgan, who was barefoot, and his brother, Frank Morgan, arrived at the scene and called for volunteers. Only Frank, Clancy, and another man, Thomas Castleberry, volunteered. [...] Of the 22 people nominated for the award, in 1917 only four were awarded the Carnegie Medal [...] Garrett and Frank Morgan were the only two Black men of the 22 nominated, and many recent publications — large and small — have claimed that Garrett Morgan was denied the Carnegie Medal because of his race. However, there is simply no evidence to support the claim. [...] it’s likely that the Hero Fund Commission’s rejection of Morgan for the Carnegie Medal was because Morgan’s own invention lessened the risk for those in his party from the “extraordinary degree” that the previous rescuers encountered.

gancho: Em 1934, a química Ida Noddack sugeriu que um núcleo de urânio bombardeado por nêutrons podia se partir em pedaços grandes. A ideia foi ignorada e ridicularizada; em 1938, a fissão nuclear foi confirmada.
explicacao: Naquele ano, Enrico Fermi bombardeou urânio com nêutrons em Roma e concluiu ter criado um elemento novo, mais pesado que o urânio. A explicação foi bem aceita por alguns anos. A alemã Ida Noddack publicou um artigo, "Sobre o elemento 93", apontando uma falha na química de Fermi: ele só tinha descartado os elementos até o chumbo, e não todos os mais leves que o urânio. E foi além: escreveu que era concebível o núcleo se quebrar em vários fragmentos grandes, que seriam isótopos de elementos conhecidos, e não vizinhos do urânio. Como a hipótese vinha sem prova experimental nem base teórica, foi ignorada e ridicularizada; Otto Hahn, entre outros, a achou ridícula. Em dezembro de 1938, o próprio Hahn e Fritz Strassmann mostraram que os supostos elementos novos eram, na verdade, bário, e Lise Meitner e Otto Frisch deram a explicação teórica do que Frisch batizou de fissão nuclear. Noddack não era uma desconhecida: com o marido, Walter, e Otto Berg, tinha descoberto o elemento 75, o rênio, e foi indicada três vezes ao Nobel de Química. Uma lei alemã de 1932 pressionava mulheres casadas a deixar seus cargos; ela seguiu trabalhando graças ao status de "colaboradora não remunerada".

fontes.trecho: In 1934 she was the first to mention the idea later named nuclear fission. With her husband Walter Noddack, and Otto Berg, she discovered element 75, rhenium. She was nominated three times for the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. [...] In 1934, Enrico Fermi bombarded uranium with neutrons in his laboratory in Rome [...] He published his findings claiming this to be evidence of a new transuranic element. [...] This theory was widely accepted for a few years. However, Noddack's paper "On Element 93" suggested a number of possibilities, but centered on Fermi's failure to chemically eliminate all lighter than uranium elements in his proofs, rather than only down to lead. [...] she suggested the possibility that "it is conceivable that the nucleus breaks up into several large fragments, which would of course be isotopes of known elements but would not be neighbors of the irradiated element." [...] However, as Noddack's theory did not exhibit experimental proof or a theoretical basis, the paper was generally ignored and mocked. Several German scientists, like Otto Hahn, saw Noddack's work as "ridiculous." [...] In 1932, a German law, replicating others in Europe, was put into place that obligated married women to leave their jobs and become housewives so that there would be more positions available for men. Noddack was able to escape this law due to her status as an "unpaid collaborator." [...] Ultimately on December 17, 1938, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann provided chemical proof that the previously presumed transuranic elements were isotopes of barium [...] Meitner and Otto Frisch utilized Fritz Kalckar and Niels Bohr's liquid drop hypothesis (first proposed by George Gamow in 1935) to provide a first theoretical model and mathematical proof of what Frisch coined nuclear fission.

gancho: Charles Drew montou bancos de plasma na Segunda Guerra e criticou a separação do sangue de doadores negros. Ao contrário de um mito famoso, ele não morreu por ter sido recusado num hospital.
explicacao: Drew (1904–1950), cirurgião negro americano, estudou a conservação de sangue em Columbia e percebeu que o plasma, separado das células, durava bem mais. No fim de 1940, dirigiu o projeto Blood for Britain, que enviava plasma ao Reino Unido: em cinco meses, quase 15 mil pessoas doaram, e mais de 5.500 frascos foram coletados. Em 1941 passou a dirigir o primeiro banco de sangue da Cruz Vermelha americana e criou as unidades móveis de coleta com refrigeração. O Exército e a Marinha primeiro recusaram o sangue de doadores negros e depois só o aceitaram guardado à parte. Drew criticou a regra, que não tinha base científica, e deixou o cargo, voltando para a Universidade Howard. A saída costuma ser contada como protesto, mas as fontes divergem sobre a data: há relatos que o põem de volta a Howard ainda em 1941, e outros que falam em 1942. Em abril de 1950, exausto depois de uma noite de cirurgias, perdeu o controle do carro a caminho de uma clínica gratuita em Tuskegee. Ele foi levado a um hospital em Burlington, na Carolina do Norte, e morreu meia hora após o primeiro atendimento. Daí nasceu a história, repetida até num episódio da série M*A*S*H, de que ele teria morrido por ser barrado num hospital de brancos. Um dos colegas que estavam no carro contou que os ferimentos eram tão graves que quase nada poderia salvá-lo. O mito pegou porque, na época, negar atendimento a negros não era raro.

fontes.trecho: Charles Richard Drew (June 3, 1904 – April 1, 1950) was an American surgeon and medical researcher. [...] Drew protested against the practice of racial segregation in the donation of blood, as it lacked scientific foundation, and resigned his position with the American Red Cross [...] It was through this blood preservation research that Drew realized blood plasma was able to be preserved two months longer through de-liquification, or the separation of liquid blood from the cells. [...] In late 1940, before the U.S. entered World War II and just after earning his doctorate [...] Drew went to New York City as the medical director of the United States' Blood for Britain project [...] The Blood for Britain program operated successfully for five months, with total collections of almost 15,000 people donating blood, and with over 5,500 vials of blood plasma. [...] Drew's work led to his appointment as director of the first American Red Cross Blood Bank in February 1941. He also invented what would be later known as bloodmobiles, mobile donation stations that could collect the blood and refrigerate it [...] The blood bank supplied blood to the U.S. Army and Navy, who initially rejected the blood of African-Americans and later accepted it only if it were stored separately from that of white people. Drew objected to the exclusion of African-Americans' blood from plasma-supply networks, and in 1942 he resigned in protest. [...] For the 1950 Tuskegee clinic, Drew drove along with three other black physicians. [...] Still fatigued from spending the night before in the operating theater, he lost control of the vehicle. [...] Drew was taken to Alamance General Hospital in Burlington, North Carolina. He was pronounced dead a half hour after he first received medical attention. [...] Despite a popular myth to the contrary, once repeated on an episode ("Dear Dad... Three") of the TV series M*A*S*H [...] Drew's death was not the result of his having been refused hospital access because of his race. According to John Ford, one of the passengers in Drew's car, Drew's injuries were so severe that virtually nothing could have been done to save him. [...] This myth spread because it was not then uncommon for black people to be refused treatment

fontes.titulo: Dr. Charles Drew: A Pioneer in Blood Transfusions (National Archives, Prologue)
fontes.trecho: In January 1941, the U.S. federal government asked the National Research Council and the American Red Cross to establish a blood program, and Drew became the director of the new American Red Cross Blood Bank. [...] Drew’s stint with the Red Cross, however, was short-lived. At the time, the Red Cross segregated blood by race even though they acknowledged there was no scientific foundation for the practice. [...] Drew resigned and returned to Freedmen’s Hospital and Howard University.

fontes.titulo: Charles Drew (1904–1950) (The Embryo Project Encyclopedia, Arizona State University)
fontes.trecho: Drew passed his American Board of Surgery exams in 1941, and returned to Howard University Hospital, which was called Freedman's Hospital at that time, as Chief of Surgery.

gancho: Em 1905, estudando larvas-da-farinha, Nettie Stevens viu que o sexo dos filhotes dependia de um cromossomo pequeno no espermatozoide, o futuro Y. O crédito costuma ir para dois homens; um deles discordava dela.
explicacao: A americana Nettie Stevens (1861–1912) notou que os machos do inseto produziam dois tipos de espermatozoide, um com um cromossomo grande e outro com um pequeno. Quando o pequeno fecundava o óvulo, nascia um macho; quando era o grande, uma fêmea. Foi a primeira vez que uma diferença visível nos cromossomos se ligou a uma característica do corpo. Outro pesquisador, Clarence McClung, achava que o cromossomo grande, hoje chamado X, definia o sexo; Stevens mostrou que o decisivo era a presença ou ausência do pequeno. Ela não deu os nomes X e Y, que vieram depois. Edmund Wilson chegou a resultados parecidos ao mesmo tempo, mas só examinou espermatozoides, não óvulos, e mais tarde, numa nota de rodapé, reconheceu que a descoberta era dela. Thomas Hunt Morgan, que tinha orientado o doutorado de Stevens, discordou das interpretações na época, mas muitas vezes recebe o crédito; em 1906, ele e Wilson foram convidados a expor a teoria num congresso, e ela não. Stevens também criou moscas-da-fruta em laboratório anos antes de Morgan adotá-las como modelo. Morreu de câncer de mama aos 50 anos, logo depois de receber a oferta do cargo de professora pesquisadora que sempre quis.

fontes.trecho: Nettie Maria Stevens (July 7, 1861 – May 4, 1912) was the American geneticist who discovered sex chromosomes. In 1905, soon after the rediscovery of Mendel's paper on genetics in 1900, she observed that male mealworms produced two kinds of sperm, one with a large chromosome and one with a small chromosome. When the sperm with the large chromosome fertilized eggs, they produced female offspring, and when the sperm with the small chromosome fertilized eggs, they produced male offspring. The pair of sex chromosomes that she studied later became known as the X and Y chromosomes. [...] Returning to the United States, her Ph.D. advisor was the geneticist Thomas Hunt Morgan. [...] She was offered the position she had long sought, as research professor at Bryn Mawr College, just before cancer took her life. [...] Her discovery was the first time that observable differences of chromosomes could be linked to an observable difference in phenotype or physical attributes [...] Stevens realized that the previous idea of Clarence Erwin McClung, that the X chromosome determines sex, was wrong and that sex determination is, in fact, due to the presence or absence of the small (Y) chromosome. Stevens did not name the chromosomes X or Y. Their current names came later. Edmund Wilson worked on spermatogenesis preparations simultaneously with Stevens's studies. He performed cytological examination only on the testes, that is he did not examine the female germ cells (eggs) but only the male germ cells (sperm) in his studies. [...] After reading the papers describing Stevens's discoveries, Wilson reissued his original paper and in a footnote acknowledged Stevens for the finding of sex chromosomes. [...] Stevens bred and studied Drosophila melanogaster fruit flies in the laboratory. She worked with these as subjects of her research for some years before Morgan adopted them as his model organism. [...] Additionally, Thomas Hunt Morgan has been credited with the discovery of sex chromosomes, although at the time of these cytological discoveries, he argued against Wilson's and Stevens's interpretations. [...] For example, Morgan and Wilson were invited to speak at a conference in 1906 to present their theories on sex determination, but Stevens was not. [...] At 50 years old, and only nine years after completing her Ph.D., Stevens died of breast cancer on May 4, 1912

gancho: A química Alice Ball tornou injetável o óleo usado havia séculos contra a hanseníase. Ela morreu aos 24 anos, em 1916, e o chefe publicou o método sem citá-la: a técnica ganhou o nome de "método Dean".
explicacao: Alice Ball (1892–1916), americana negra, fez mestrado em química no College of Hawaii e foi a primeira mulher e a primeira pessoa negra a concluir o curso ali, em 1915. Um médico da estação de pesquisa sobre hanseníase do Havaí, Harry Hollmann, pediu ajuda com o óleo de chaulmoogra, o melhor tratamento disponível havia centenas de anos. O problema era a aplicação: engolido, dava náusea e vômito; injetado, era viscoso demais e causava feridas sob a pele. Ball converteu os ácidos graxos do óleo em ésteres etílicos, que se misturam à água e podem ser injetados e absorvidos pelo sangue. Ela morreu aos 24 anos, em dezembro de 1916, antes de publicar. O químico Arthur Dean, que fora seu orientador e dirigia o college, continuou os testes e publicou o trabalho sem citá-la, e a técnica ganhou o nome de "método Dean". Em 1920, um médico relatou que 78 pacientes tinham recebido alta de um hospital do Havaí após as injeções. Em 1922, Hollmann publicou um artigo dando o crédito a Ball e chamando a técnica de "método Ball". O tratamento não curava, mas foi o único eficaz até as sulfonas dos anos 1940. A Universidade do Havaí só a homenageou em 2000.

fontes.trecho: Alice Augusta Ball (July 24, 1892 – December 31, 1916) was a Black American chemist whose groundbreaking work produced the first effective treatment for Hansen's disease, better known as leprosy. [...] While working in Hawaiʻi, Ball was approached by Harry T. Hollmann of the Leprosy Investigation Station [...] Ingested doses caused nausea and vomiting, while injectable forms caused painful lesions under the skin. Ball's critical innovation was developing a method to chemically modify chaulmoogra oil's fatty acids into ethyl esters, making the compound water-soluble and suitable for injection. [...] allowed the drug to be absorbed into the bloodstream safely and efficiently [...] Ball died unexpectedly in 1916 at age 24 before she could publish her findings. [...] Chaulmoogra oil had been the best treatment available for leprosy for hundreds of years, and Ball developed a much more effective injectable form. In 1915 she became the first woman and first Black American to graduate with a master's degree from the College of Hawaii. [...] Arthur L. Dean, a chemist and Ball's graduate study advisor, dean of the college, and later president of the university, was privy to details of the process she developed. After Ball's death, Dean undertook further trials [...] Dean published details of the work and the findings without acknowledging Ball as the originator or crediting her work. Her name is not mentioned in any of Dean's published works on the chaulmoogra extract, while the name "the Dean method" is appended to the technique. In 1920, a Hawaii physician reported in the Journal of the American Medical Association that 78 patients had been discharged from Kalihi Hospital by the board of health examiners after treatment with injections of Ball's modified chaulmoogra oil. [...] While not curative or able to fully halt the disease's progress indefinitely, the isolated ethyl ester remained the only available, effective treatment for leprosy until sulfonamide drugs were developed in the 1940s. Ball's colleague Hollmann attempted to correct the mistaken impression of the extract's development. He published a paper in 1922 giving credit to Ball, calling the injectable form of the oil the "Ball method" throughout the article. [...] Ball died on December 31, 1916, at age 24. [...] the University of Hawaiʻi honored Ball in 2000 by dedicating a plaque to her

gancho: A enfermeira Jean Purdy foi a primeira a ver se dividir o embrião que viraria Louise Brown, o primeiro bebê de proveta. Em 1980, uma placa sobre a técnica omitiu o nome dela, apesar dos protestos de Robert Edwards.
explicacao: Purdy (1945–1985) era enfermeira em Cambridge quando, em 1968, virou assistente de pesquisa do fisiologista Robert Edwards, que se juntava ao ginecologista Patrick Steptoe para tentar a fertilização fora do corpo. Ela registrava cada caso de forma sistemática e às vezes tocava o laboratório sozinha; quando se afastou para cuidar da mãe doente, o trabalho teve de parar. Em 1974, desanimado com a falta de resultados e de verba, Edwards cogitou desistir, e, segundo uma amiga de infância de Purdy, foi ela quem o encorajou a continuar. Purdy foi a primeira a ver se dividir o óvulo fecundado que daria origem a Louise Brown e, segundo o obituário no Times, a primeira a descrever a formação do blastocisto humano. Louise Brown, o primeiro "bebê de proveta", nasceu em 25 de julho de 1978. Purdy ajudou a fundar a clínica Bourn Hall, assinou 26 artigos com os dois colegas e morreu de melanoma aos 39 anos. Em 1980, a placa planejada para celebrar a técnica saiu sem o nome dela, e os protestos de Edwards foram rejeitados. Ele insistiu: "Havia três pioneiros da FIV, não dois". O Nobel de 2010 foi só dele, porque o prêmio não é dado a quem já morreu. Uma placa com os três nomes só foi inaugurada em 2015.

fontes.trecho: Jean Marian Purdy (25 April 1945 – 16 March 1985) was a British nurse, embryologist and pioneer of fertility treatment. [...] Louise Joy Brown, the first "test-tube baby", was born on 25 July 1978, and Purdy was the first to see the embryonic cells dividing. [...] In 1968, she took the position of research assistant to the physiologist Robert Edwards at the Physiological Laboratory in Cambridge. In 1968, Edwards began to collaborate with obstetrician and gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe [...] Purdy systematically recorded the essential details of each case. [...] Purdy regularly worked away from home, sometimes managing the lab alone. [...] when she took time off to care for her sick mother, work had to pause. [...] In mid-1974, Edwards became depressed by a lack of progress and funding [...] According to Purdy's childhood friend Rosemary Carter, Purdy asserted her support for the IVF project and encouraged Edwards to continue their research. It was Purdy who first saw that a fertilised egg cell was dividing to make new cells. According to Purdy's obituary in The Times, Purdy was the first person to identify and describe the formation of human blastocysts. [...] Purdy was a co-author on 26 papers with Steptoe and Edwards [...] On 16 March 1985, Purdy died at the age of 39 in Addenbrooke's Hospital from melanoma. [...] Edwards was awarded the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on the development of in vitro fertilisation; however, because the Nobel Prize is not awarded posthumously, neither Purdy nor Steptoe were eligible for consideration. In 1980 a plaque was planned to honour the development of IVF. The plaque's text, as approved by administrators, excluded Purdy's name. Edwards protested against this omission but his objections were rejected by an administrator. [...] "There were three original pioneers in IVF and not just two". [...] In 2015, Professor Andrew Steptoe of the Royal Society of Biology (Patrick Steptoe's son) unveiled a blue plaque that acknowledged the three people involved in developing IVF.

gancho: Pagando a vidraria com um empréstimo pessoal, a médica Marthe Gautier montou um laboratório de cultura de células e viu, em 1958, o cromossomo a mais da síndrome de Down. A autoria ainda é disputada.
explicacao: Em 1956, pesquisadores suecos anunciaram que os humanos têm exatamente 46 cromossomos. Em Paris, o chefe de Gautier, Raymond Turpin, suspeitava havia anos de uma origem cromossômica para a síndrome de Down, e ela, que tinha aprendido cultura de células em Harvard, se ofereceu para contar os cromossomos. Com poucos recursos, montou do zero um laboratório de cultura de células in vitro: pagou vidraria com um empréstimo pessoal e às vezes usou o próprio sangue como fonte de soro. Em maio de 1958, viu um cromossomo extra nas células de um menino com a síndrome. Como o hospital não tinha microscópio capaz de fotografar, ela confiou as lâminas a Jérôme Lejeune; segundo Gautier, ele não as devolveu e apresentou a descoberta como sua. O artigo de 1959 saiu com Lejeune como primeiro autor e ela em segundo, com o sobrenome escrito errado. A fundação que leva o nome de Lejeune contesta essa versão e diz que foi ele quem identificou o cromossomo. Em 2014, a fundação obteve autorização judicial para mandar oficiais de justiça filmarem uma palestra de Gautier sobre o caso, e os organizadores a cancelaram. Meses depois, o comitê de ética do Inserm, o instituto francês de pesquisa médica, lamentou que o nome dela não tenha sido sempre associado à descoberta.

fontes.trecho: In 1956, biologists from Lund University in Sweden announced that humans have exactly 46 chromosomes. Turpin had many years earlier proposed the idea of culturing cells to count the number of chromosomes in trisomy. Gautier had recently joined the pediatrics group he headed at the Armand-Trousseau Hospital, and she offered to attempt this, since she had been trained in both cell culture and tissue staining techniques in the United States. [...] With very limited resources Gautier set up the first in vitro cell culture laboratory in France. [...] who was forced to use a personal loan to purchase laboratory glassware and, at times, her own blood as a source of human serum. [...] In May 1958, she observed an additional chromosome in the cells of a trisomic boy, the first evidence of chromosomal abnormalities in individuals with Down syndrome. [...] At the time, the laboratories at the Armand-Trousseau hospital did not have a microscope capable of capturing images of the slides. Gautier entrusted her slides to Jérôme Lejeune [...] In January 1959, by studying new cases and to forestall similar research by the English [...] However, according to Gautier's account, Lejeune did not return the slides, but instead reported the discovery as his own. [...] through a paper published with Lejeune as first author, Gautier second (her surname misspelled as Gauthier) and Turpin last author. [...] The Jérôme Lejeune Foundation asserts that a letter from Turpin to Lejeune in October 1958 shows that Lejeune, and not Gautier, identified the 47th chromosome. [...] The Jérôme Lejeune Foundation obtained authorisation from the Bordeaux Tribunal de Grande Instance for bailiffs to be sent to film this session. At the last minute, concerned that the recording might be used in legal proceedings it could not afford to defend, the congress organizers decided to cancel her presentation [...] The ethics committee of the Inserm has issued a note in July 2014, reminding of the decisive role of Marthe Gautier [...] it is regrettable that their names were not systematically associated with this discovery

gancho: Os desenhos da patente do telefone de Graham Bell foram feitos por Lewis Latimer, filho de pessoas que fugiram da escravidão. Depois ele melhorou filamentos de lâmpadas para um rival de Edison e para o próprio Edison.
explicacao: Os pais de Lewis Latimer (1848–1928) fugiram da escravidão na Virgínia para Boston em 1842. O pai foi preso logo depois, e o caso virou bandeira abolicionista, com apoio de Frederick Douglass; a liberdade dele foi comprada com dinheiro arrecadado por um pastor. Aos 16 anos, Latimer se alistou na Marinha. Depois virou office boy num escritório de patentes, aprendeu sozinho a usar esquadro e régua e chegou a desenhista-chefe. Em 1876, Alexander Graham Bell o contratou para fazer os desenhos exigidos para patentear o telefone. Em 1879, foi trabalhar na empresa de iluminação de Hiram Maxim, rival de Thomas Edison, e criou um processo que reduzia a quebra dos filamentos de carbono das lâmpadas: os filamentos eram embrulhados num envelope de papelão durante a carbonização. Em 1884, entrou na companhia de Edison como desenhista e perito em disputas de patentes, escreveu em 1890 o primeiro livro sobre iluminação elétrica incandescente e, em 1918, foi a primeira pessoa negra aceita entre os Edison Pioneers. Também patenteou um precursor do ar-condicionado e um sanitário para vagões de trem, e escrevia poesia.

fontes.trecho: Lewis Howard Latimer (September 4, 1848 – December 11, 1928) was an American inventor and patent draftsman. His inventions included an evaporative air conditioner, an improved process for manufacturing carbon filaments for electric light bulbs, and an improved toilet system for railroad cars. [...] Before his birth, his parents escaped from slavery in Virginia and fled to Boston in October 1842. Shortly after their arrival, George Latimer was arrested under the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793, and his case became a widely publicized abolitionist cause. Prominent antislavery figures, including Frederick Douglass and William Lloyd Garrison, publicly supported the effort to prevent his return to Virginia. George Latimer ultimately secured his freedom after a local Black minister, Samuel Caldwell, raised funds to purchase his release. [...] On September 16, 1864, at the age of sixteen, Latimer enlisted in the United States Navy [...] he gained employment as an office boy with a patent law firm [...] He learned how to use a set square, ruler, and other drafting tools. Later, after his boss recognized his talent for sketching patent drawings, Latimer was promoted to the position of head draftsman [...] In 1876, Alexander Graham Bell employed Latimer, then a draftsman at Bell's patent law firm, to draft the necessary drawings required to receive a patent for Bell's telephone. In 1879, he moved to Bridgeport, Connecticut, and was hired as assistant manager and draftsman for the US Electric Lighting Co., a company owned by Hiram Maxim, a rival of Thomas Edison. [...] Latimer also developed a forerunner of the air conditioner called "Apparatus for cooling and disinfecting". [...] On February 11, 1918, Latimer joined the Edison Pioneers, becoming the first person of color to do so. [...] a method for the production of carbon filaments for light bulbs which reduced breakages during the production process by wrapping the filaments in a cardboard envelope. The Edison Electric Light Company in New York City hired Latimer in 1884 as a draftsman and an expert witness in patent litigation on electric lights. While at Edison, Latimer wrote the first book on electric lighting, entitled Incandescent Electric Lighting (1890) [...] A book of poetry called Poems of Love and Life.
